Its formation follows a White House meeting where OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang were among industry leaders agreeing to voluntary principles covering model monitoring, independent reviews and board-level safety notifications.

Investing.com -- Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the U.S.-Iran war has been an economic "disaster," blaming the conflict for higher inflation and borrowing costs and warning that it is weighing on global growth, Bloomberg reported.
"Whatever the reasons were for going in, from an economic point of view the war in the Middle East has been a disaster," Chalmers told ABC News’ Insiders program on Sunday.
Chalmers said higher costs stemming from the conflict were affecting Australians and consumers elsewhere, with upward pressure on inflation contributing to higher interest rates globally. His comments come after Australia’s central bank raised interest rates to a 15-year high in an effort to curb inflation, citing elevated energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict alongside domestic capacity pressures.
Chalmers rejected suggestions that government spending was the primary driver of Australian inflation, saying spending growth had slowed.
The government is preparing a savings package for its mid-year budget update. Chalmers warned that rising global bond yields would add "some billions of dollars" to the government’s debt-servicing costs.
He said intensifying borrowing-cost pressures were affecting government budgets globally, with the final impact on Australia’s fiscal position still uncertain.
Chalmers said Australia was not anticipating a recession but warned that weaker global growth from the conflict would also affect the domestic economy.
Separately, Chalmers said he would travel to Japan on Sunday to meet Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, business leaders and investors.

title: Apple to flag AI requests for Mac data after Meta’s Muse complaints
full_text:

Investing.com -- Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) said it plans to change its Mac operating system to make it clearer when artificial intelligence agents request access to all data stored on a computer, Reuters reported Friday.
The move follows complaints about Meta Platforms’ (NASDAQ:META) Muse AI agent, which can perform complex tasks such as cancelling unused subscriptions and negotiating lower prices. Some users claimed Muse accessed messages they believed were private.
Apple’s iPhones and iPads use sandboxing, which prevents individual apps from accessing data inside other apps by default. Macs offer greater flexibility through a "Full Disk Access" setting that allows applications such as cloud backup services to access all data on a machine with user permission.
Apple said some developers were using the feature in ways that could expose users to risks.
The company plans to introduce additional controls requiring users who want to give an application that level of access to take a more explicit action.
"As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said.
The company said it wants users to understand the potential risks before granting applications access to their data.
Apple’s announcement follows claims by Inc magazine technology columnist Jason Aten that Muse read private messages stored on his Mac. Aten said he had not enabled Full Disk Access.
Meta spokesperson Andy Stone disputed the claims last week, saying access to Apple’s Messages app through Muse is strictly opt-in.
Stone said users must enable both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector before Muse can read Messages content. He added that users can revoke that permission at any time.
Apple declined to comment beyond its published statement. Meta did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
The changes put additional attention on operating-system permissions as increasingly autonomous AI agents gain the ability to perform tasks across applications and access information stored on users’ devices.

Investing.com -- Wall Street’s focus on Friday was on the September nonfarm payrolls report which showed significantly weaker-than-expected job growth, prompting traders to pare their expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month.
As per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls rose 29k last month, significantly lower than the estimated figure of 89k. The monthly growth was the slowest of the year. Moreover, nonfarm employment in July and August combined were revised down by 60k. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
The data comes at a time when separate indicators have suggested a resilient U.S. economy and a slight moderation in stubbornly high inflation. Any signs of labor market weakness in such a scenario means a central bank would typically hold interest rates steady, as tightening policy can quell price pressures but at the risk of further denting economic growth and labor activity.
The reaction in Fed October rate expectations reflected the same. As per the CME FedWatch tool, the odds of a quarter-point rate hike later this month fell to nearly 22% while those of the central bank holding rates steady surged to about 78%.
Wall Street and the U.S. Treasury bond market caught a bid after the jobs report. The enthusiasm faded slightly later in Friday’s session, with U.S. stocks paring some gains and yields rising again. The 10-year Treasury yield was last up 3.4 basis points to 5.272%.

See below for various reactions to the jobs data:
Dan Alpert, executive chairman at Westwood Capital:
“This was a miss that will take pressure off the Fed and the bond market. Equities rallying on bad news = good news.”
Michael Feroli, chief U.S. economist at JPMorgan:
“Nonfarm employment increased only 29,000 last month, and the gains for the prior two months were revised down by a net 60,000. That left the 3-month average gain at 51,000 last month, which is close to most estimates of trend monthly growth in the labor supply, i.e. breakeven job growth.
Wage growth has been decelerating, a trend which continued last month as average hourly earnings were up only 0.1% for the month and 3.0% over a year ago. That deceleration should give comfort to Fed policymakers that the economy is not overheating in a way that calls for a hurried rate hike cycle.
It would now take a very strong CPI to make the October meeting live. We continue to look for another hike at the December FOMC meeting, on the assumption that the September and October price reports show still-sticky trends in core inflation.”
Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial:
“We are seeing the tension between the goods-producing sectors that support the AI boom and the services-producing sectors that are feeling the impact of technological change. Given the overall softness of the labor market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is getting lower.”
Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial:
“There is zero chance for a rate hike in October now—in retrospect, September should have been a hold. Outside of energy, the inflation impulse is lower, and Fed was zigging when it should have been zagging.”
Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG U.S.:
“The Fed is (expected) to skip a rate hike in October and resume hikes in December. They are trying to prevent a larger blow to the labor market and engineer a softer landing. Still, the inflation data going into the October meeting will be ugly and hot due to the resurgence of energy prices. Elevated diesel prices could have a long tail, given the loss in global refining capacity due to the war in Ukraine and conflict in the Middle East.”
Joseph Brusuelas, principal and chief economist at RSM US:
“The low hire, low fire U.S. jobs market remains our baseline forecast and one should anticipate the soft pace of hiring to continue going forward. Statistically insignificant noise is the primary reason for the modest uptick in unemployment and full employment remains the best description of the American labor market currently.
The soft pace of hiring and noise around the size of the domestic labor force should support those at the Federal Reserve looking to keep the federal funds policy rate on hold at the upcoming October meeting. The September data implies little to no risk of second round wage induced inflation and the fact of the matter is that the Fed is simply not worried about the employment side of their mandate at the current time.
Our baseline call on the direction of monetary policy remains no hike in October and one twenty-five basis point hike in December and then another in March of 2027.”
Justin Wolfers, professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan:
“An all around weak -- but not tragic -- payrolls report for September.”

Investing.com -- Hong Kong share sales raised a record $47.5 billion in the third quarter as Chinese technology companies tapped investors for capital to fund artificial intelligence expansion, Bloomberg reported.

Investing.com -- The FlyDubai copilot accused of attacking the captain of a Tel Aviv-bound flight previously worked for Oman Air before being dismissed over engagement with views considered radical, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the situation.

Investing.com -- Britain’s growing reliance on U.S. cloud providers for critical public services poses a "strategic and economic vulnerability," lawmakers warned, as concerns mount over Washington’s potential legal authority over data and services, Bloomberg reported.
UK government departments spend about £1 billion ($1.3 billion) annually on cloud services, according to parliamentary committee estimates. Amazon Web Services and Microsoft may account for as much as 80% of government cloud purchases, though officials do not know the precise level of dependence.
Chi Onwurah, chair of parliament’s science, innovation and technology committee, raised concerns over the U.S. CLOUD Act. Experts told the committee that U.S.-headquartered providers could be compelled to disclose data stored on their servers or withdraw services under certain circumstances.
The issue has gained urgency as health, defence, and tax services migrate to U.S.-owned cloud platforms.
HM Revenue & Customs awarded AWS a £473 million, 10-year contract to manage UK tax data in the past year. Britain’s defence ministry signed a £400 million agreement with Google Cloud, and National Health Service trusts are moving patient records from servers to U.S. cloud providers.
Government departments said their data was protected in UK-based data centres and contracts were subject to security and data protection requirements.
Onwurah said Britain was unlikely to build a domestic competitor capable of matching the largest U.S. providers and suggested greater cooperation with France and Germany.
European governments are already pursuing alternatives. France replaced Microsoft Azure with domestic provider Scaleway for its national health data hub in April, and Germany’s Schleswig-Holstein has shifted from Microsoft products towards open-source alternatives.
The European Commission is also developing a framework intended to increase Europe’s cloud and AI sovereignty.
The UK government said it was working to strengthen resilience and improve public-sector cloud procurement, with departments required to consider risks associated with excessive dependence on individual suppliers.

Voter frustration has grown over an economic slowdown, the slow pace of EU entry talks and a lingering political crisis in which the ethnically based dominant parties from the two entities have repeatedly stalled decisions by the weak central government that links them.
Bosnia, which has struggled to recover from the bloody 1992-95 war, secured EU candidate status in December 2022 and the green light to open accession negotiations in 2024. Actual talks have not started because domestic political leaders have yet to enact core requirements such as bolstering judicial oversight and passing anti-corruption laws.
Preliminary results are expected to be released by the Central Election Commission after polls close at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Sunday.
The Bosnian war ended in 1995 with the US-brokered Dayton peace accord, which left the country split along ethnic lines into the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation — linked by the central government and tripartite presidency.
Many voters in the country of 3.4 million people say they want to move beyond the divisive rhetoric, but the politics appears stuck.
Dusan Cvijic, a 76-year-old pensioner from Banja Luka, the largest city of the Republika Srpska, said the government’s policies failed. “What has been done so far has been inadequate. If ethnically based parties prevail and continue their bickering within the central government, which would be the body that would eventually officially join the EU, progress on accession is likely to be stalled further.
In the capital, Sarajevo, Ismar Garasljevic, a 51-year-old high school teacher, said: "More than 30 years after the war, the situation is still the same; we are talking about nationalism ... The same faces, the same story, constantly."
Voters on Sunday will face redesigned ballots alongside new biometric voter identification and electronic scanners introduced to curb voting fraud.
US AND RUSSIAN INFLUENCE
Major powers have long sought influence over Bosnia. The EU is seeking to expand its membership across the Balkans, including Bosnia, but Russia is slowing it down, maintaining its support of the Republika Srpska.
The US has also sought to gain influence and wants to push for a $1.5 billion pipeline project to import US liquefied natural gas, run by a company with links to the Trump administration, but the EU warned that the company selection lacked competitive transparency.
Washington has also clashed with Brussels over the role of the international High Representative, who, under provisions of the Dayton accord, enforces the laws. Christian Schmidt, a former German government minister, resigned in May under pressure from the US.

Agents can search hotels and other suppliers directly, potentially reducing the advantage Booking and Expedia gain from aggregating inventory. They can also prioritise customers’ preferences rather than inventory generating higher commissions.

Price discovery represents another threat. Booking and Expedia brands offered the cheapest hotel rate only about 15% of the time in U.S. searches examined in 2026. Smaller OTAs supplied the lowest price 77% of the time, creating an opportunity for agents capable of searching across more providers.
Current technology still offers Booking and Expedia some protection. Chat-based agents are less suited to complex hotel searches involving maps, amenities and multiple filters, and large OTAs provide agents with extensive inventory from a single source.
Airbnb appears better positioned. About 70% of its nine million active listings are estimated to be exclusive to the platform, limiting agents’ ability to find identical properties elsewhere. Airbnb also receives about 45% of web traffic directly, reducing its dependence on paid search.
Its customer relationship also extends beyond booking. Around 90% of guests message hosts after making a reservation, giving Airbnb additional opportunities to retain users on its platform.
The revenue model adopted by AI agents could determine the eventual impact. User-funded agents seeking unbiased results pose the greatest threat to OTAs, whereas advertising-supported models could preserve more of the existing travel distribution economics.

The court’s 6-3 conservative majority has moved US law dramatically rightward in recent years.
The top US judicial body, as is its custom, opens its term on the first Monday in October.
US-based Exxon and Canada-based Suncor appealed after the Colorado Supreme Court let Boulder’s lawsuit accusing them of state law violations proceed. The Trump administration has backed Exxon and Suncor, arguing that federal law precludes Boulder’s claims.
Boulder’s city and county governments have accused the two companies of helping drive climate change and misleading the public about the risks of fossil fuels. Boulder aims to hold the companies liable for past and future costs associated with climate change such as infrastructure repairs, environmental damage, emergency management and harms to public health.
The burning of fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases including carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, trapping heat and raising average global temperatures over time.
Nearly 60 state and local governments have brought similar suits seeking billions of dollars from fossil fuel companies, with more continuing to be filed, Exxon and Suncor told the justices. A ruling by the Supreme Court in favor of the companies could lead to many of those cases being dismissed.
Monday’s arguments mark the latest example of energy-sector companies asking the justices to block climate-related liability or limit federal environmental regulation.
Backers of the oil companies argue that if Boulder’s most far-reaching claims are allowed to proceed, it could give states sweeping power over conduct occurring far outside their borders.
Energy companies and trade groups, along with states allied with them, have built a largely winning record before the justices over the past two decades in cases involving climate liability and the reach of federal environmental regulation.
Exxon and Suncor argue, among other things, that Boulder’s claims intrude on an area governed by the Clean Air Act.
Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from participating in the case. Alito owns stock in several oil and gas companies but not Exxon or Suncor, according to his financial disclosure forms.

In the US, where Revolut has a provisional license, it will face tougher competition, investors said.

A striking measure of its growth is customer numbers.

Revolut’s website shows it has 80 million customers, against 84 million for JPMorgan and 41 million for HSBC.

Revolut makes far less from each of its customers than traditional banks, a Reuters analysis of its figures shows. Average deposit balances are also much lower.
Lower per-customer revenue is in part because Revolut lends much less than traditional banks, instead relying on fees such as card subscriptions.
With just £2.2 billion in loans at end-2025, Revolut’s loan-to-deposit ratio of 6% compares with 55% for HSBC and 86% for Societe Generale.
Scaling its lending business will introduce risks including managing big and complex credit exposures, while entering fiercely competitive local mortgage markets will not be easy, analysts and investors said.

Revolut has attracted customers with its easy-to-use app but executives acknowledge too few use it as a primary bank account.
Revolut declined to comment in its latest results on how many customers did so in 2025, but said the figure was up 45% from a year ago.
This metric is a focus for Revolut’s biggest backers.
Alex Immerman, an investor at Andreessen Horowitz, which is known as "a16z", told Reuters it was watching for primary-account adoption, as well as total customer balances.

ADEN, Oct 4 (Reuters) - The leader of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced the beginning of a major military operation against the Iran-backed Houthis on Sunday, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Regional and western officials had told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia, claiming the attacks caused major fires, in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes on Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
’OPPORTUNITIES FOR DE-ESCALATION EXHAUSTED’
Al-Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted, accusing the Houthis of responding to efforts to calm the conflict with further mobilisation and escalation.
"Our position today is to assume the national responsibility of confronting the Houthi militia, after all opportunities for de-escalation have been exhausted," he said.
Al-Alimi said he had ordered the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under approved plans.
Saudi Arabia entered neighbouring Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognised government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa.
Al-Alimi thanked Saudi Arabia for its support, saying the kingdom had "stood alongside Yemen in the darkest circumstances," and called on Yemen’s regional allies and international partners to support the country, its armed forces and state institutions.
The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.
A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.
HOUTHIS’ LIGHTNING OFFENSIVE
The Houthis have so far maintained the initiative on the ground, weeks after seizing the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in a lightning offensive down the coast that saw government forces collapse.
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.
The Houthis already controlled the northwest of the country, where most of the population live.
In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen’s Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast, where the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is based.
Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen’s third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.
It would also consolidate control of that flat coastal Bab el-Mandeb area by seizing the rugged mountains overlooking them in the western Taiz countryside, according to Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist from Taiz now working as a political analyst.
"This will help them protect their back in case of any operation against the coastline, and make recapturing those areas much more difficult," he said.
The city is important not just for its strategic location; Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.
Three-in-four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

title: Explainer-Who are the Houthis, Iran’s allies in Yemen?
full_text:

Oct 4 (Reuters) - Yemen’s Saudi-backed government announced the start of a military counteroffensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, aimed at seizing the territory under their control.
Renewed warfare between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has reignited Yemen’s frozen civil war and heightened risks to Red Sea shipping, further disrupting Middle Eastern energy exports already choked by Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.
WHO ARE THE HOUTHIS?
The Houthis are a military, political and religious movement that rules over most of northwest Yemen and has disrupted global trade and energy markets with attacks on cargo ships and tankers in the Red Sea.
It began firing on ships in the Red Sea and launching drones and missiles at Israel in November 2023, saying it was doing so in support of Palestinians during Israel’s war in Gaza that began the previous month.
Those attacks on Red Sea shipping, as well as on Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States’ war on the Houthis’ close ally Iran.
WHAT DO THE HOUTHIS WANT?
The group emerged in far north Yemen in the 1990s as a revival movement for the Zaydi sect of Shi’ite Islam, which had once ruled Yemen but whose northern heartland had become impoverished and marginalised.
It fought a series of guerrilla wars against Yemen’s national army and a brief border conflict with Sunni Saudi Arabia.
When Yemen’s longtime president Ali Abdullah Saleh was brought down in the 2011 "Arab spring" protests, the group consolidated its control over northern Yemen, rejecting a Gulf-backed political transition.
With Iranian support, the group’s secretive leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, was meanwhile turning his faction of mountain fighters into a force of tens of thousands.
In 2014 they seized the capital Sanaa, driving the internationally recognised government south towards Aden.
WHAT’S BEHIND THE HOUTHI CONFLICT WITH SAUDI ARABIA?
Fearful of growing Iranian influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to dislodge the group, restore the government and revive the transition plan.
The resulting civil war triggered one of the world’s biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of bitter fighting and devastating airstrikes by Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners, including the United Arab Emirates.
However, neither side was able to gain much ground in Yemen’s mountainous terrain, and the Houthis remained in control over the northwest, where most of the population lives.
They demonstrated significant missile and drone capabilities, attacking oil installations and vital infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
After years of fighting, the UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year.
HOW MUCH DAMAGE CAN THE HOUTHIS DO WITH ATTACKS IN THE RED SEA AND SAUDI ARABIA?
The group’s attacks on Red Sea shipping between 2023 and 2025 significantly disrupted global trade, forcing cargo ships travelling between Europe and Asia to take a long, expensive route around Africa.
Their threats to oil tankers during the Iran war have added to the squeeze on energy out of the Gulf after Tehran mostly choked off the Strait of Hormuz, adding to a global oil crisis.
Some Houthi missile and drone attacks have caused significant damage in Saudi Arabia and the UAE over the years, but have proven less effective against targets further north, such as Israel.
LINKS WITH IRAN
Iran champions the Houthis as part of its regional "Axis of Resistance", which also includes Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Iraqi Shi’ite militias, though its ties with the Yemeni movement are less clear than with those other groups.
The Houthis do not recognise Iran’s supreme leader as their ultimate religious authority in the same way Hezbollah and the Iraqi groups do. Their motivations are also mainly domestic, though they are ideologically aligned with Iran.
The US says Iran has armed, funded and trained the Houthis with help from Hezbollah. The Houthis deny being an Iranian proxy and say they develop their own weapons.

title: Spiking bond yields, midterms, earnings to test US stocks’ typical fourth-quarter strength
full_text:

By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Investors head into a part of the calendar that tends to be upbeat for US stocks, but that seasonal strength is under threat from a number of challenges, including a surge in bond yields and the market’s apparent dependence on massive AI spending.
As the fourth quarter kicks off, the stock market is already on pace for a solid year. The benchmark S&P 500 as of Friday had gained nearly 13% in 2026, and sat about 1% below its mid-August record high.
Markets face a busy end of 2026, with the start of corporate earnings season and a pivotal Federal Reserve meeting in coming weeks, along with the looming November 3 midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.
"It does tend to be a seasonally strong period, however I think this year investors are facing some headwinds as we go into the fourth quarter," said Tracie McMillion, head of global asset allocation strategy at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
Q4 TENDS TO SEE STOCK GAINS
Since 1945, the S&P 500 averaged an increase of 4.2% in the fourth quarter, with the index posting gains 85% of the time, according to research firm CFRA. That average percentage rise is more than twice that of the other three quarters.
Fourth quarters of midterm years have generally been even stronger, with an average gain of 6.4%, as stocks "benefit from the lifting of election uncertainty," Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA, said in a note.
While fourth quarters tend to shine, mid-term years overall historically have been subpar, a trend stocks have defied so far in 2026. The S&P 500 has averaged a 15% dip in midterm years historically, while the deepest drop so far this year has only been 9%, according to McMillion of the Wells Fargo institute.
The firm is on "high alert" for a pullback between now and election day, she said, for example, if it looks like the Democrats can wrest full control of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republican party.
"If we were to see a change in the leadership in the House and the Senate combined, then we think that that could have some policy ramifications that could impact the markets," she said, while adding that a pullback could be a buying opportunity.
SPIKING YIELDS IN FOCUS, FED MINUTES DUE
The most immediate issue for stock investors is the jump in bond yields. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield on Thursday hit 5.34%, its highest level in 24 years. Yields, which rise when bond prices fall, have soared amid expectations for strong economic growth, surging energy costs that are driving up inflation, and increased competition for capital as companies issue debt to fund AI expansions.
Higher yields likely already are impeding the market’s advance, investors said. They can create more investment competition for equities and pressure stock valuations, while translating into more expensive borrowing costs throughout the economy.
"The interest rate story is the biggest headwind," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services. "You’re going to need some relief on that front. I don’t necessarily think the market will tank per se, but to get a meaningful rally in the face of that, I think is going to be a struggle for the market."
Another factor driving yields is the Fed’s plans for monetary policy. The US central bank hiked interest rates last month for the first time in three years in an effort to cool above-target inflation. Minutes covering that meeting will be released on Wednesday and could offer Wall Street clues about the Fed’s rate outlook, including the potential for another hike in October or December. Following weaker-than-expected jobs data on Friday, markets kept bets that the Fed would likely hold off on a second straight hike at its meeting later in the month.
BIG EARNINGS GROWTH SEEN, AI SPEND IN SPOTLIGHT
PepsiCo and Delta Air Lines are among the handful of large companies set to post third-quarter results next week, before major banks kick off the reporting season more broadly the following week.
This year, corporate profits have surpassed already-lofty projections, propelling the stock market’s rally. But they have also raised the bar for stellar performance that could test the market. S&P 500 companies overall are expected to have increased earnings by more than 30% in the third quarter from a year earlier, according to LSEG IBES data.
Particularly important are developments related to the massive spending by AI hyperscalers to build out infrastructure, which has lifted profits at a wealth of companies.
The US stock market’s performance has been highly correlated to the AI theme, said Nelson Yu, head of equities at AllianceBernstein.
As it relates to AI this upcoming earnings season, "the number one thing to watch for is capex revisions from the hyperscalers," Yu said. "Because that does kind of start the whole chain."

US LNG projects approved since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have generally been built at an average cost of about $1 billion per mtpa or less.

title: How Brazil’s election winner could reshape its institutions as vacancies mount

By Marcela Ayres and Ricardo Brito
BRASILIA, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Brazil’s next president is set to inherit an unusually large number of appointments to the country’s most powerful institutions, with vacancies piled up at the Supreme Court, central bank and economic regulators.
The growing backlog of unfilled posts means the winner of the tight race between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro could gain significant influence over bodies that help shape monetary policy, oversee financial markets and interpret the constitution. The two candidates will face off in the first round of the electoral contest on Sunday, with a runoff later in the month forecast as the most likely outcome.
The vacancies reflect a broader shift in Brazilian politics: an increasingly powerful Congress is using confirmation of nominees as a tool for political leverage, eroding the executive branch’s room for maneuver.
A predominantly right-wing Congress has flexed this growing power during Lula’s current term by delaying confirmation of a number of his nominees. Lula has also failed to make some nominations.
While nominations once went promptly to Senate committees for approval, many nomination processes stalled during the pandemic, awaiting the Senate president’s approval. Senate President Davi Alcolumbre has maintained that practice, concentrating power in the Senate and turning what was once a routine step into a political decision, said a person familiar with the process, who requested anonymity.
The presidential palace and Alcolumbre’s office did not respond to requests for comment.
The use of presidential appointments as political leverage has made the executive reluctant to submit nominees without first gauging their Senate prospects, said Rubens Beçak, a law professor at the University of Sao Paulo.
BANK SEATS
At the central bank, two board seats, including the economic policy post that oversees forecasts ahead of rate decisions, have been empty since January, a record length of time for those posts to be left open. Lula has yet to submit nominees.
In April, senators rejected Lula’s Supreme Court nominee, Solicitor General Jorge Messias, in a historic setback that extended a vacancy now nearly a year old, the longest since Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s.
Securities regulator CVM has had board vacancies since late 2024, while antitrust watchdog Cade, lacking its president and two board members, is near its minimum quorum, delaying merger reviews.
Claudio Couto, a political scientist at the Fundacao Getulio Vargas, called the backlog "deeply problematic," saying it risks concentrating appointments in one administration and politicizing "bodies that are meant to remain nonpartisan."
STRUCTURAL SHIFT
Nominations and bills, once largely negotiated between the president and coalition parties, increasingly hinge on deals among congressional leaders, said Neuriberg Dias, head of legislative watchdog DIAP.
Congress’ growing control over spending, he said, has changed the incentives behind executive-legislative bargaining.
Congressional earmarks — which direct funding to local or pet projects — accounted for 7.5% of effective federal discretionary spending in 2018, but swelled to 21% in 2025, according to Planning Ministry data provided to Reuters.
The government’s grip on the agenda has in turn weakened. Last year, Congress approved 178 bills introduced by legislators and only 50 from the executive. In 2007, during Lula’s second term, the reverse was true: 142 executive bills versus 52 from Congress, according to DIAP data.
The 2026 campaign has slowed nominations further, people familiar with the matter said, as lawmakers wait to see whether Lula wins another term. Voters will also elect all 513 members of the Lower House and two-thirds of the Senate.
With power shifting from the presidency to Congress, the election may decide not only who governs Brazil, but how much room the winner will have to appoint officials and shape key institutions.

Oct 4 (Reuters) - OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman said the benefits of artificial intelligence justify accepting some risks and argued the technology should remain broadly accessible to the public
"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," Altman said in an interview with Politico’s technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Altman said there remained a fundamental difference in worldview between OpenAI and rival Anthropic on AI regulation, adding: "I think there’s a lot of daylight."
"I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ’This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,’" Altman said.
He called that "a completely unacceptable trade-off" that runs counter to the "lighter-touch regulatory stance" backed by OpenAI.
"I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ’We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen,’" Altman said. "Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff."
Altman’s remarks come amid a growing debate within the AI industry over the pace of development and the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September published an essay calling on the industry to slow down to "pace the frontier," a stance that Altman publicly endorsed. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September, saying the people building AI believe it "could kill us all by the end of the decade.

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs maintained its “sell” rating on Adobe as Anil Chakravarthy prepares to take over as president and CEO on Dec. 1, saying competition is intensifying and new entrants are gaining ground in areas that could expand Adobe’s market.
The broker said it wants clearer evidence of Adobe’s strategy and execution before changing its view. It sees the leadership change as a potential catalyst, but said the market remains concerned that artificial intelligence could weigh on Adobe’s growth.
Chakravarthy’s appointment follows a transition announced in March. He previously led Adobe’s Customer Experience Orchestration business and worldwide field operations. David Wadhwani, who headed the Creativity & Productivity business, is also leaving to start a new venture, while Adobe is appointing a permanent chief financial officer.
Goldman said a successful turnaround will depend on Adobe simplifying its product architecture, speeding up innovation through internal investment and targeted acquisitions, and converting adoption of new features into revenue. The key question is whether the new management makes significant strategic changes or largely extends the existing three- to five-year plan.
Goldman highlighted five areas to watch:
Firefly: Adobe has shifted from relying mainly on its own Firefly models toward using Creative Cloud as a platform that brings together multiple third-party AI models. 
Goldman said this moves Adobe’s focus from competing on AI model quality to controlling the workflow. Firefly initially stood out because its models were trained on Adobe Stock, licensed content and public-domain material.
Acquisitions: Goldman expects Adobe to pursue smaller deals that add technology and engineering talent rather than make a large transformational acquisition. 
It pointed to Salesforce and Workday as examples of companies taking a similar approach, although potential targets could command high valuations.
User growth: Monthly active users across Acrobat, Creative Cloud, Express and Firefly exceeded 1 billion in the third quarter, up more than 20% from a year earlier. 
Adobe is seeking to turn that growth into revenue through free-to-paid conversions, higher-priced plans such as CC Pro and charges for users who exceed their included generative AI credits.
Express: Goldman said Adobe’s uneven product development has left Express trailing Canva, which has more than 265 million monthly users and at least $4 billion in annual recurring revenue. Goldman estimated Express had about 70 million monthly users in 2025.
Customer experience: Adobe is repositioning Experience Cloud, which accounts for about a quarter of subscription revenue and is growing at a low-teens rate excluding Semrush, as a platform for managing AI-driven customer experiences.
